title: Fama-French 1992 redux with optimal robust regression

p.s: Introduction
p.t: Concern for possible outliers influence on Fama-MacBeth (FM) least-squares (LS) cross-section regressions is evident in the asset pricing literature. For example Fama and French (2008) expressed the generic concern ". . . because the returns on individual stocks can be extreme, the potential for influential observation problems lurks in FM regressions." and the microcap specific concern that "regressions estimated on all stocks can be dominated by microcaps because they are so plentiful and because they tend to have more extreme values of the explanatory variables and more extreme returns". Likewise Hou et al. (2020) state that: "Hundreds of studies perform cross-sectional regressions of returns on anomaly variables, mostly with ordinary least squares, which are highly sensitive to microcap outliers". In order to deal with the problem of extreme values and outliers (Fama and French 2008) suggest to avoid the problem ". . . by estimating separate regressions for microcaps, small stocks, and big stocks, as well as for a sample that includes factor exposure outliers adversely influence LS Size regressions, and thereby result in misleading conclusions about the Size factor for the vast majority of the cross-section of stocks. Relatively recent treatments of robust regression in accounting, empirical asset pricing, and time series factor models quantitative finance are provided in Leone et al. (2019), Gu et al. (2020), and Martin and Xia (2022), respectively. Leone et al. compare the performance of a robust regression estimator, similar to the one we propose herein, with Winsorization, and conclude that the robust regression is preferred. Gu et al. (2020) integrate a well-known Huber robust regression estimator objective function into some machine learning methods. More recently (Martin and Xia 2022) discuss an "mOpt" optimal bias robust regression estimator for returns time series factor models, and provide a variety of application examples showing that the mOpt estimator provides better model fits than least square (LS). These authors also show that the Huber regression estimator is lacking in robustness as much as the LS estimator for time series models with predictor variable outliers.

p.s: Introduction
p.t: The "m" in "mOpt" indicates that the estimator is a regression M-estimator, which stands for "maximum-likelihood type" estimator. This terminology was introduced long ago in the seminal (Huber 1964) paper on robust estimation of a location parameter. The "Opt" refers to the estimator's optimality property that it minimizes the large-sample bias due to outliers. Furthermore, for normally distributed data the mOpt regression estimator is unbiased, and has a variance only very slightly larger than that of the LS estimator. The mOpt estimator has a weighted least squares (WLS) form with intuitive data-dependent weights that very effectively control for outliers. Specifically, it rejects as outliers those stock returns and factor exposure pairs for which robustly scaled regression residuals are greater than 3.0 in magnitude. Extensive mathematical details of the mOpt regression estimator are readily available to the interested reader in Martin and Xia (2022), which was published as Open Source. 1 In this paper we use the mOpt estimator to determine the premia and significance of the Size, BM, Beta and EP factors, in comparison with the well-known least squares regression results of Fama and French (1992), henceforth FF92. We recall that FF92 reported that for the 1963-1990 time period: (1) Size alone is significant with a negative premium; (2) BM alone is significant with a positive premium; (3) Size and BM are collectively significant, with negative and positive premiums respectively; (4) Beta is not significant; (5) EP alone is significant with a positive premium, but is insignificant when included with Size and BM. 2 By way of sharp contrast, our mOpt robust regression results for that time period are that: (1) Size alone is significant, but with a positive premium, thereby reconfirming the KR97 result; (2) BM alone is significant with a positive premium; (3) Size and BM are collectively significant, but the Size premium is positive; (4) Beta alone is significant with a negative premium; (5) EP alone is significant with a positive premium, and EP remains significant when included with Size and BM.

p.s: Introduction
p.t: We also study the comparative mOpt and LS based premia and significance of the FF92 Size, BM, Beta, and EP factors for the time period 1980-2018, and present those results in parallel with the 1963-1990 for ease of comparison. Roughly speaking our mOpt results relative to LS are similar for the two time periods. We also made such comparisons for a number of shorter contiguous time periods to determine the extent to which factor significance was subject to regime change effects. The reason for the difference between our robust regression results and the FF92 least squares results is that the latter are quite adversely influenced by small fractions of outliers. The overall cross-section percentage of outliers rejected by our robust regressions is 3.45%, when averaged across the Size, BM, Beta and EP factors and the time period 1963-2018. In spite of such small percentages, outliers have a huge adverse influence on LS regressions based factors significance and premia, but have little influence on the corresponding mOpt results. The over-arching results of this paper are that it is good statistical practice to always compute well-justified robust regressions as a complement to LS regressions. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section "Robust mOpt regression for the Fama-MacBeth method" describes the mOpt robust regression estimator, the resulting robust Fama-MacBeth method, and the data sources and treatment used for this study. "Fama-French single factor models robust mOpt versus least squares" presents our mOpt versus LS single factor significance and premia results for the FF92 time period 1963-1990 and for 1980-2018, along with graphical displays that reveal the impact of outliers on LS factor returns and cross-section regressions, and tabulation of the frequency of outliers rejected by the mOpt regression. "Multifactor models mOpt versus least squares" presents mOpt versus LS factor significance and premia for the four factor Size, BM, Beta and EP model, and all subsets of two and three factor models for 1963-1990 and 1980-2018. "Regimes based factor models analysis" does likewise for the single factor and four-factor models for five time periods that appear to be different regimes of factor behavior. "Market capitalization group analysis of mOpt and LS results " presents an analysis of mOpt versus LS results for separate microcap, smallcap and bigcap stock groups, and for a combined smallcap and bigcap group. "Summary and open issues" provides a summary and brief discussion of open issues. The Appendices contain supplemental details.

However, for simplicity and based on the Harvey et al. statement ". . . that a newly discovered factor today should have a t-statistic that exceeds 3.0.", we refer to factors with an absolute t.hac of at least 3.0 as a significant factor. A reason to consider the "newly discovered factor" aspect relevant is that mOpt robust regression analysis of factor significance is quite new, and leads to conclusions that are quite different than published conclusions based on least squares. For descriptive purposes we call factors whose absolute t.hac value between 2.0 and 3.0 as weakly significant, and in need of further study.

p.s: Data sources and treatment
p.t: The stock returns and firm financial data needed for the factors in our study are from the CRSP ® and Compustat data bases maintained by Wharton Research Data Services (WRDS). 5 We constructed the Size, BM and Beta factor values exactly as in FF92 using all non-financial firms. Further details and factor exposures formulas are provided in Appendix A. Whereas FF92 used positive earnings to price (EP+) and a dummy for negative earnings to price (EPND), our study used unaltered earnings to price (EP). For purpose of replicating the FF92 least squares results we follow their practice of Winsorizing the BM and EP variables at 0.5%, and for the sake of consistency we do so for all of our LS analysis. Unfortunately, such Winsorization can be quite inadequate for subsequent LS analysis, and it turns out that this is especially so for EP. Fortunately, this is not an issue for the mOpt robust estimator, which deals quite adequately with outliers in factors and returns, and so we do not Winsorize factors when fitting cross-section factor models with mOpt. When we discuss results related to stock market capitalization groups, we follow the Fama and French (2008) and Hou et al. (2020) convention of defining microcap, smallcap and bigcap stocks using the NYSE 20% and 50% breakpoints, where the bigcap stocks consist of the combination of midcap, largecap and megacap stocks. efficiency, where efficiency is defined as the ratio of the variance of the least squares coefficients to the variance of the robust regression coefficients. It can be shown that the w mOpt (x) tuning constant value c = 3.0 results in a normal distribution efficiency of 95%. 3 It is fairly common practice to use robust estimators that have a 95% normal distribution efficiency. On the other hand one may wonder how sensitive inference results are to the choice of this efficiency. In this regard, Appendix B shows that using alternative normal distribution efficiencies of 99% and 90% have little impact on conclusions drawn from inference results presented in the remainder of the paper .

p.s: Robust Fama-MacBeth and choice of t-statistics significance threshold
p.t: The classic Fama-MacBeth method is a two step procedure, based on preliminary computation of time series dependent factor exposures such as Beta, price momentum (PM), etc.,, where the first step computes a least squares crosssection factor model of the form (1) for each month, thereby obtaining K time series of factor returns (regression slopes) θk,t , t = 2, • • • , T, k = 1, 2, • • • , K. The second step consists of computing an HAC corrected t-statistic for each of the K time series θk,t , where the t-statistic for judging the significance of the k-th factor exposure is based on the time series sample mean μk = T -1 ∑ T t=1 θk,t of the regression slopes. Our robust Fama-MacBeth regressions are obtained by replacing the least-squares estimates θk,t with mOpt robust estimates. All mOpt regressions in this paper were computed with the function lmrobdetMM in the R package RobStatTM available at CRAN, where by default lmrob-detMM uses the mOpt weight function of Fig. 1. We note that many studies based on Fama-MacBeth regressions fit cross-section regression models using exposures that are standardized by subtracting the exposures sample mean and dividing by their standard deviations. This makes results for different factors comparable, and leads to a useful dollar neutral portfolio characterization of the slope estimates. However, this is not necessary for inference concerning the regression slopes, so for simplicity we do not do such standardization.

p.s: Robust Fama-MacBeth and choice of t-statistics significance threshold
p.t: The time series θk,t typically suffer from heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation, and it is common practice to use a heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation correction (HAC) correction in order to obtain accurate t-statistics. 4 In this The over-arching results for 1963-1990 revealed by Table 1 are that while the mOpt robust regression estimator results for BM agree quite closely with the FF92-LS results, the mOpt regressions result in significantly different conclusions than the FF92-LS for the Size and Beta factors. The Size columns for 1963-1990 show that instead of the FF92-LS negative average slope of -0.15 and t.iid statistic value of -2.58, the mOpt robust regression results in a positive average slope of 0.37 and the quite large t.hac value of 7.30. Although these Size results will be surprising to many who have taken the FF92 negative Size premium as the common wisdom, very similar robust regression results for Size had already been demonstrated in the KR97 study that used a least-trimmed squares (LTS) robust regression method, and revealed that the negative Size effect of FF92 was mostly due to small stocks. It is striking that their results have been quite ignored in the empirical asset pricing literature. We conjecture that one reason for this may be the perceived ad hoc nature of the LTS regression method, whose breakdown point is equal to the trimming fraction.

p.s: Robust Fama-MacBeth and choice of t-statistics significance threshold
p.t: As for the Beta factor during 1963-1990, the FF92-LS t.iid statistic value of 0.46 in the Beta column of Table 1 led to the FF92 conclusion that Beta does not explain the cross-section of returns. However, our mOpt robust regression t.hac value of -4.87 for that time period indicates a strong negative relationship between returns and Beta. This result contrasts with the discussion in Chapter 8 of Bali et al. (2016) that existing research indicates that there is either a weak negative relationships or no relationship between Beta and the cross-section of expected returns, depending on the Beta factor estimation method. 6 Finally, for the EP factor during 1963-1990 our LS t.hac value of 1.04 indicates that this factor lacks significance and does not explain the cross-section of expected returns, but the mOpt t.hac value of 3.09 indicates that EP is a significant factor and expected returns are positively related to EP. 6 See in particular Table 8.6 in Bali et al.

p.s: 1963-1990 Results for mOpt versus FF92 LS
p.t: We focus first on 1963-1990 results, where the FF92-LS row contains the least squares results as reported in FF92 for Size, BM and Beta (but not EP since FF92 used EP+), the LS row contains our least squares results, and the mOpt row contains our mOpt robust regression results. The columns of the table display the following for each of the four factors: the sample mean of the time series of regression slopes (Mean), the corresponding classical t-statistics based on assuming the time series of slopes are independent and identically distributed (t.iid), and the Andrews HAC adjusted t-statistics (t.hac). We provide our LS results in addition to the FF92-LS results in order to show that when using the same data, data treatment, and least squares fitting as in FF92-LS, we get essentially the same statistical results, and correspondingly the same conclusion as FF92-LS for Size, BM and Beta. This led us to have confidence in the data acquisition and factor computations aspects of our overall comparative study of mOpt robust regression versus LS regressions for the FF92 models. Note that for the 1963-1990 results in Table 1, the absolute value of the t.hac is always less than the value of t.iid for our LS and mOpt results, sometimes considerably so. p.s: 1980-2018 Results for mOpt versus LS
p.t: Our least squares LS t.hac results for 1980-2018 in Table 1 are very similar to those for 1963-1990, with BM the only one of the four factors that explains the cross-section of returns based on a t.hac threshold of 3.0. Furthermore, the 1980-2018 mOpt robust regression t.hac values are all highly significant, with values for Size, Beta and EP factors that are substantially larger in absolute value than those for 1963-1990. Thus the overall explanatory power of the four factors for 1963-1990 persists even more strongly for 1980-2018. p.s: Two-factor and three-factor models mOpt versus LS
p.t: As an initial exploration of all possible two-factor and threefactor multiple factor fits, without regard to the important topic of model selection, we compared mOpt and LS fits of adverse influence on the LS estimator. The percentages of outliers rejected by the March 1986 robust cross-section regressions for Size, BM, Beta and EP, shown in the legends of Figs. 3, 4, 5 and 6, are 4.95%, 4.41%, 3.73% and 5.11%. One naturally wonders how typical these percentages are, so we computed the percentages for all the months in our study, and display their time series averages for the 1963-1990 and 1980-2018 periods in the Allcap row of Table 2. We also broke downs the averages according to market capitalization groups and display those time series average percentages of outliers in the Microcap, Smallcap and Bigcap rows. Recall from "Robust mOpt regression for the Fama-MacBeth method" that for normally distributed regression model errors, the outlier rejection probability is only 0.27%, with respect to which all the time series average percents of outliers rejected in Table 2 are quite huge. The primary source of the of outliers is clearly the microcaps Table 2 shows that the Size and EP regressions consistently give rise to larger overall percentages of outliers than the BM and Beta regressions. It is notable that all the outlier percentages increase in the 1980-2018 time period relative to 1963-1990. While the primary source of outliers is clearly the microcaps, we will show in "Market capitalization group analysis of mOpt and LS results" that removal of microcaps does not solve the problem of outliers influencing factor t.hac values, and that infrequent outliers can adversely influence t.hac values even for portfolios of only bigcap stocks.

p.s: Two-factor and three-factor models mOpt versus LS
p.t: The primary source of the of outliers is clearly the microcaps. However, it turns out that the much smaller percentages of outliers in smallcap and bigcap stocks can nonethe-less have substantial adverse influence on LS based factor significance and premia. The validity of this claim is substantiated in Table 3 is similar to Table 2, except that now the variable used is the outlier stocks monthly value as a percent of the significant. For the mOpt three-factor regressions during the second time period, all three factors are significant except for the BM, Beta and EP model, where once again BM is not significant. It is interesting that for both time periods BM fails to be significant when included with Beta and EP. As was the case in the two-factor mOpt fits, the Beta premium is negative in all the three-factor fits. On the other hand, the mOpt robust regressions for 1963-1990 result in BM being significant in just two of the three models in which it appears, while Size and EP are significant in all three models in which they appear, and Beta is significant in only the BM+Beta+EP model. For the 1980-2018 period, Size, Beta and EP are significant in all three models in which they appear, and it is striking that BM is not significant in the BM+Beta+EP model, where EP supplants BM, and this is also the case for the 1963-1990 period. Furthermore, for both time periods EP is significant in the Size+BM+EP model, which is quite the opposite of the FF92 LS conclusion that EP is not significant when included with BM and Size. p.s: Two-factor and three-factor models mOpt versus LS
p.t: For the mOpt robust two-factor regressions it is striking that all pairs of factors are significant in each of the twofactor models, often highly so, for both time periods. The Size+BM pair have particularly large t.hac values of 9.23 and 10.55 for 1963-1990, and 17.55 and 12.22 for 1980-2018. Furthermore, the Beta premium is negative for all pairs of factors in which it appears. For the mOpt robust three-factor regressions during the first time period, the only model for which all three factors are significant is the model with Size, BM and EP, and it is interesting that for the BM, Beta and EP model BM is not very nearly significant with a surprising negative t.hac value of -2.93. At first we thought that the startling negative t.hac value for BM was only due to the financial crisis period of 2007-2008 and its 2009-2010 after-effects. So we repeated the analysis for the period 2011-2018 after the financial crisis effects had died out, and it turned out that the mOpt regression inference conclusions for all four of the factors do not change much relative to those of 2007-2018. In particular, BM for 2011-2018 still has a negative premium with a significant t.hac value -3.32. This result is of course not totally surprising given recent literature on the demise of BM as a value factor, for example as in Arnott et al. (2021) and a number of references therein.

p.s: Two-factor and three-factor models mOpt versus LS
p.t: For the multifactor fits in Table 8, the LS regressions result in a significant factor only for BM in the 1976-1989 regime with a typical positive t.hac value, and for EP in the 1990-2006 with the quite unusual negative t.hac value -4.23. Not surprisingly. the mOpt robust regression results in more occurrences of factors with significant t.hac values. But there is little consistency in the subsets of mOpt significant factors across different regimes: in the first, second, third and fourth regimes, respectively, the following different subsets of factors are significant with mOpt: (1) Size and EP, (2) Size, BM and EP, (3) Size and BM, (4) Size and EP.

p.s: Regimes based factor models analysis
p.t: So far we have only provided analysis results concerning which of the four factors are significant for the 28 year FF02 period 1963-1990 and the longer 39 year period 1980-2018. While the results for the second period are reasonably consistent with those of the first period, analysis over multiple shorter periods is in general called for, e.g., as in the Black (1993) use of decade intervals to evaluate his beta factor. We have already noted that the time series of mOpt and LS slopes and their differences exhibit non-stationarity and this is especially evident for the EP slopes differences in Fig. 2, which exhibit several distinctly different temporal regimes of behavior. In particular, the time intervals 1963-1975, 1976-1989, 1990-2006 and 2007-2018 represent a reasonable set of regimes for fitting factor models separately for each regime. 11 The mOpt and LS results for doing so are displayed in "Four Regimes" groups in Tables 7 and 8 for the single-factor and four-factor models, respectively. For the single-factor models in Table 7 with a t.hac threshold of 3.0, the only factor that is significant for LS is the BM factor during the second and third regimes and nearly so for the first regime. On the other hand for the mOpt regressions, all four factors are significant for the second, third and fourth regimes, except for BM in the fourth regime where BM is 11 One might argue for somewhat different time segmentation, for example among other possibilities, the 1990-2006 may deserve to be split into two intervals. However, the intervals we have chosen here will suffice for this initial study of robust mOpt versus LS performance on relatively short time intervals. The results in Table 10 for 1980-2018 are as follows: (a) For the microcap group: the conclusions with regard to factor significance and premium are identical to those for 1963-1990 in Table 9, except that the mOpt t.hac values are larger; (b) For the smallcap group: for LS no factor is significant and only BM and EP are weakly significant, and for the mOpt all four factors are significant with the Beta premium negative; (c) For the bigcap group: among the LS regressions, no factors are even weakly significant, and among the mOpt regressions no factor is significant, but Beta and EP are weakly significant.

p.s: Regimes based factor models analysis
p.t: Based on the differences between mOpt and LS t.hac values, we can conclude from the above capitalization group analysis that: (1) For 1963-1990 outliers influence on LS estimates is quite substantial for both microcap and smallcap stocks, and for bigcap stocks outliers influence is not substantial. (2) For 1980-2018 outliers influence on LS estimates is somewhat substantial for the Beta and EP factors.

p.s: Market capitalization group analysis of mOpt and LS results
p.t: Table 2 shows that the largest percentage of influential outliers rejected by the mOpt regressions occur for microcaps, with considerably smaller percentages of such outliers occurring in the smallcap and bigcap stock groups. One thus might think that removal of microcap stocks may solve the problem of outliers influence on LS cross-section analysis. We will show that this is not the case by examining the mOpt and LS t.hac and factor premia values for each the microcap, smallcap and bigcap stock groups separately for 1963-1990 and 1980-2018, and then doing likewise for the combined smallcap and bigcap stocks.

p.s: mOpt and LS results for separate microcap, smallcap and bigcap stock groups
p.t: The results in Table 9 for 1963-1990 are as follows: (a) For the microcap group: among the LS regressions the only factors that are significant are Size (with a negative premium) and BM, and there are no weakly significant factors, and among the mOpt regressions all four mOpt factors are significant and Beta has a negative premium; (b) For the smallcap group: among the LS regressions the only significant factor is BM factor and the only weakly significant factor is t.hac values, which goes against the "common knowledge" that the Size premium is negative; (2) For both robust and LS regressions the BM factor results are consistent with the FF92 LS positive premium results until the time period 2007-2018, by which time BM was commonly viewed to be no longer a value factor; (3) As for Beta, our finding with robust regression, but not with LS, is that beta is significant with a negative premium, which is quite at odds with the FF92 finding that beta does not explain the expected value of the cross-section of returns 12 ; (4) Finally, for the EP factor the robust regressions have consistently significant t.hac values with a positive premium, both alone and with BM. 13 Finally, a notable finding of our study is that microcap stocks account for the bulk of the influential outliers rejected by the mOpt regressions. For example, Table 2 shows that across all four of the factors from 1980 to 2018, the average percent of all stocks whose data was rejected as outliers is 4.0%, and the microcap stocks subset percent was 3.3%. The above outlier percentages, combined with the fact that few investors include microcaps in their portfolios, suggest that microcaps can be ignored in cross-section factor models studies such as that herein. Furthermore, the Bigcap rows of Table 10 show that outliers are essentially not a problem for least squares analysis of the Bigcap combination of midcap, largecap and megacap stocks. However, the Table 11 results for the combined Smallcap and Bigcap groups, i.e., the cross-section of stocks with only the Microcaps removed, show that Smallap outliers are still a problem. So unless one is focused only on Bicap stocks, robust regression is needed for dealing with outliers.

p.s: mOpt and LS results for combined smallcap and bigcap stocks group
p.t: The 1963-1990 results for the combined Smallcap and Bigcap groups in Table 11 are mixed in that for LS only BM is significant and only EP is weakly significant, while for mOpt only EP is significant and BM and Beta are weakly significant, the latter with a negative premium. On the other hand the 1980-2018 results in Table 11 reveal a striking difference between the mOpt and LS results: For LS none of the factors are significant and only EP is weakly significant, but for mOpt the Size, Beta, and EP factors are significant, and BM is weakly significant. The over-arching conclusion is that removal of microcaps does not solve the LS lack of robustness problem. This is because when included with bigcaps, smallcaps have sufficient influential outliers to adversely influence the LS estimates. Furthermore, recalling the 1980-2018 results for the Bigcap group only in Table 9, where the LS t.hac values for Beta and EP are quite insignificant while the mOpt t.hac values are weakly significant, we conclude that one also needs to be concerned about outliers influence on LS estimates for the Bigcap group by itself.

p.s: Summary and open issues
p.t: In re-visiting the FF92 results for the Size, BM, Beta and EP factors, we have made the case for using a theoretically justified mOpt robust regression method that optimally controls for bias due to outliers, and performs very nearly as well as LS for normally distributed data. Our study shows that Fama-MacBeth LS regressions, which are completely lacking in robustness toward outliers, result in factor significance and premia conclusions that are often dramatically different than those obtained with mOpt robust Fama-Mac-Beth regressions that reject small fractions of influential outliers. Our main findings are: (1) With robust regression the Size factor premium is positive, with highly significant Meanwhile, it is our hope that this article will stimulate use of mOpt robust regression in financial factor models research as a standard practice, along with transparent reporting on the extent to which the influential outliers impact the analysis. An exemplar of such reporting would be to report either: A robust regression check revealed no significant outliers influence on the least squares regressions. or for example in the case of the Size factor herein: Using least squares, the Size premium is negative for the specified cross-section of U.S. stocks, and using robust regression the Size premium is positive due to rejection of an average during 1980-2018 of abpit 4.7% of the stocks, whose joint returns and factor exposures are outliers. About 4.5% of rejected stocks are either microcap or smallcap stocks, and only 0.2% are bigcap stocks.

p.s: Summary and open issues
p.t: And similarly for other factors separately and jointly in multi-factor models. of influential outliers that result in such differences. Analyses for this purpose can benefit considerably by use of insightful graphical displays, chief of which in this article are the hexbin plots of returns versus factor exposures in Figs. 3 through 6. Hexbin plots have the generally useful feature of representing the probability density of the data in high density regions, while at the same time revealing isolated outliers in low density regions. Thus one is able to see the individual outliers data rejected by mOpt regressions as those data points falling outside the region defined by the parallel dotted lines in those figures. The rejected outliers in the upper left of the Fig. 3 Size factor plot are of particular interest with respect to the fact that the LS estimate of the Size premium is negative, whereas the mOpt estimate Size premium is positive. This is because the outliers in the upper left region of the plot, for small firms with large returns, result in biasing the LS slope estimate in a negative direction, whereas the mOpt slope is not influenced by these rejected outliers. Our study herein leaves open a most important question raised by a reviewer, namely: What is the extent to which mean-variance optimal portfolios computed using returns covariance matrix estimates based on robust regression fits of cross-section factor models, have better performance than those fitted with least squares? After all, the fact that robust regression fits lead to factors that are more or less significant, or have different signs, than those fitted with least squares, does not in any way insure that robust regression fitting of factor models leads to better mean-variance optimal portfolio performance than least squares fitting. Unfortunately, to the best of our knowledge there exist no meaningful research studies of this issue.

p.s: Summary and open issues
p.t: Since there are at most only a few published results focused on use of robust regression in empirical factor significance research, it is not surprising that there currently exist no studies on the comparative effectiveness of robust versus least squares cross section factor models regression in improving mean-variance optimal portfolio performance. On the other hand, the need for such studies is underscored by the "on the street" common knowledge that the portfolio solutions provider Axioma uses a robust regression method (called the Huber method) in their commercial product. In this regard, a simple query to ChapGPT leads to a view of the 2017 document "Axioma RobustTM Risk Model Version 4 Handbook" that contain details of the method. Since many Axioma customers are presumably using that robust regression method, it is all the more striking that there are no studies of the impact of robust regression on the performance of mean-variance optimal portfolios. Such a study is long overdue, and would be an important complement to our results herein. for the entire period, and is assigned to its component stocks at each month.
